title: Defective DNA Repair Syndromes
subject: Pathology
summary: Inherited defects in DNA repair predispose to early‑onset cancers and multisystem disease. Recognising the clinical pattern, basic investigations and management is essential, especially where advanced testing is limited.

sections.p: DNA repair syndromes are inherited conditions where mutations impair the ability of cells to correct DNA damage, leading to genomic instability and cancer predisposition.
b: Diagnosis relies on clinical phenotype, family history and, when available, genetic testing for known repair genes.

sections.p: Severity is gauged by organ involvement, age of cancer onset and presence of bone‑marrow failure.
b: Mild: isolated cancer risk, no marrow failure.
Moderate: marrow cytopenias, early‑onset solid tumours.
Severe: pancytopenia, multiple malignancies, endocrine failure.

sections.p: Most common autosomal‑recessive DNA‑repair defects in low‑resource settings are:
b: Fanconi anemia – interstrand cross‑link repair defect.
Ataxia‑telangiectasia – ATM‑mediated double‑strand break repair.
Bloom syndrome – RecQ helicase defect, high sister‑chromatid exchange.

sections.p: Patients often present in childhood or early adulthood with a combination of:
b: Growth retardation, skin hyperpigmentation or café‑au‑lait spots.
Congenital anomalies (thumb abnormalities in Fanconi, telangiectasias in AT).
Recurrent infections from marrow failure.
Early‑onset leukaemia, lymphoma or solid tumours.

t.b: Detects cytopenias indicating marrow failure – low neutrophils, platelets or red cells.
Confirms Fanconi anemia by increased chromosomal breaks after DNA cross‑linker exposure.

t.a: Serum AFP and ß‑hCG (if tumour suspected)
t.b: Screens for germ‑cell tumours common in DNA‑repair syndromes.

t.a: Targeted gene panel or whole‑exome sequencing
t.b: Identifies pathogenic variants in FANCA, ATM, BLM, etc.

sections.p: Rapid decline in blood counts, new lymphadenopathy, unexplained bruising or persistent fever demand urgent evaluation.
b: Acute myeloid leukaemia – marrow blast >20%.
Severe aplastic anaemia – pancytopenia with hypocellular marrow.
Solid tumour with rapid growth – may need urgent imaging.

sections.p: Treatment focuses on preventing complications, managing marrow failure and treating malignancy.
b: Hematopoietic stem‑cell transplant for severe marrow failure (curative when donor available).
Avoid DNA‑cross‑linking chemotherapy (e.g., cyclophosphamide) in Fanconi patients; use non‑alkylating agents when possible.
Supportive care: transfusions, infection prophylaxis, iron chelation for transfusional overload.
Cancer therapy: surgery when feasible, radiotherapy with caution (high radiosensitivity), targeted agents if tumour harbours actionable mutation.
Annual CBC and physical exam for early leukaemia detection.
Bi‑annual ultrasound or MRI of abdomen for solid tumours.
Genetic counselling for family members; prenatal testing where culturally acceptable.

sections.p: Conditions that share skin findings or cytopenias.
b: Neurofibromatosis type 1 – café‑au‑lait spots but no marrow failure.
Severe combined immunodeficiency – infections without DNA‑repair defect.
Congenital aplastic anaemia – marrow failure without cancer predisposition.

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely reassuring.
b: Normal CBC does not exclude early marrow stress; repeat if clinical suspicion persists.
Chromosome breakage test may be normal in mosaic Fanconi cases – consider repeat with higher drug dose.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden drop in haemoglobin or platelets

faq.q: Why are DNA‑repair defects linked to cancer?
faq.a: Unrepaired DNA damage accumulates mutations, driving uncontrolled cell growth.
Heterozygous carriers usually remain asymptomatic but may have modestly increased cancer risk.
Yes, if the pathogenic variant is known; it can guide early counselling.

exam: What bedside clues would make you suspect a DNA‑repair syndrome in a 12‑year‑old with bruising? — Look for growth delay, skin pigment changes, thumb anomalies, and family cancer history.

A patient with Fanconi anemia needs chemotherapy for AML. Which agents should you avoid and why? — Avoid alkylating agents and cross‑linkers because their cells cannot repair the induced DNA breaks, leading to excess toxicity.
How would you prioritize investigations when genetic testing is unavailable? — First obtain CBC, then chromosome breakage test, and finally refer for imaging if malignancy is suspected.

Explain why radiotherapy doses must be reduced in ataxia‑telangiectasia. — AT patients lack ATM‑mediated double‑strand break repair, making them highly radiosensitive and prone to severe tissue injury.
What is the definitive curative option for severe marrow failure in Fanconi anemia? — Allogeneic hematopoietic stem‑cell transplantation from a matched donor.

A child with Bloom syndrome presents with early‑onset lymphoma. Which supportive measures are essential before chemotherapy? — Correct any cytopenias, provide antimicrobial prophylaxis, and assess organ function to tolerate treatment.
How does the chromosome breakage test differentiate Fanconi anemia from other marrow failures? — Only Fanconi cells show markedly increased breaks after exposure to diepoxybutane or mitomycin C.

What counselling would you give a sibling of a diagnosed patient about cancer screening? — Recommend regular clinical exams, CBC monitoring, and consider genetic testing if the familial mutation is known.
